messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi is a 29-year-old shopowner who lives with his partner in a midsized Midwestern city. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his partner’s urging, after months of escalating distress that he had tried to manage on his own. He is South Asian, the son of immigrants, and runs a small convenience store in a working-class neighborhood. His PCL-5 score of 80 reflected the severity of what he had been carrying alone.

The traumatic event had occurred nearly eighteen months earlier, in the apartment he had shared at the time with his former partner, a man named Derek. What began as an argument over something trivial—Ravi could no longer remember what—had escalated into physical violence. Derek had shoved him against the kitchen counter, then grabbed him by the collar and slammed him onto the tile floor. Ravi had not fought back. He had not screamed. He had lain there, staring at the ceiling, while Derek’s body weight pressed down on him, the sour smell of sweat and stale beer filling his nostrils. He remembered thinking, *If I just stay still, it will stop.* And it did stop, eventually. But that moment—the pressure, the smell, the helpless stillness—had never truly ended.

In the months that followed, Ravi’s life contracted slowly, almost imperceptibly at first. He began to notice the smell of sweat or body odor on customers who came into his store, and each time it happened, his chest would tighten, his hands would go cold, and the memory would surge back without warning. He could be ringing up a sale, handing change to a stranger, and suddenly he was back on that kitchen floor. Sometimes the rage came with it—a hot, blinding fury at Derek, at himself, at the world—and he would have to excuse himself to the back room, gripping the sink until his knuckles whitened. Other times, the emotion arrived without any image at all: a wave of terror or shame that washed over him while he stood in the cereal aisle, leaving him disoriented and breathless, with no clear reason why.

Certain conversation topics had become minefields. When customers or friends mentioned relationships, arguments, or even casual frustrations with partners, Ravi would feel his throat close. He had learned to steer conversations away, to nod and change the subject, to keep his own story locked inside. He was certain that if anyone knew what had happened—if they knew he had let himself be hurt without fighting back—they would see him as weak. He could not rely on himself, he had come to believe. His body kept reacting as if the danger were still present, even when he was safe in his own apartment with the door locked. At night, the vigilance was worse. He slept poorly, waking at every creak of the building, every footstep in the hallway, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. He had begun checking the locks three times before bed.

The guilt was the heaviest weight. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened—for not pushing Derek away, for not leaving earlier, for not seeing the signs. In his quieter moments, he told himself that he should have been stronger, should have known better. That he had failed himself.

His avoidance had reshaped his daily life. He stopped going out after dark, even for groceries. He avoided strangers on the street, crossing the road when someone approached, his shoulders tensing until they passed. He had stopped seeing friends altogether, canceling plans with excuses about the store. His partner had grown worried, then frustrated, then frightened for him. It was she who finally said, *You can’t keep living like this.* And so Ravi had come, not because he believed talking would help, but because he was tired of being afraid in his own skin. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to stop feeling like a stranger to himself. What he feared was that he already was one.
